Players in Brazil and Japan chat in the same game and messages must arrive in under a second. The chat service detects language, checks a cache of common phrases, sends to a translation service, an ML model sharded by language pair, applies safety and slang filters, and returns translated text to each recipient in their language. Messages stream through a queue, latency stays around 300 ms, with fallback to the original text and feedback collection. I'd handle game slang with glossaries and evaluate with human bilinguals.

s.t: AI strategy, metrics and product thinking
q: You own an internal AI platform that other teams build agents on. What is your strategy and what is the one metric you own?

Ten teams build agents on ten stacks and quality and cost vary. My strategy is to make the platform the easiest and safest path: treat internal builders as customers, standardise the model gateway, evals, tool and MCP registry, guardrails and observability, provide templates, reduce time to first agent and enforce safety centrally. The one metric I'd own is the number of agents in production that meet the quality bar each quarter, or time from idea to production, paired with guardrails on cost and incidents. Teams ship faster with consistent quality.
How would you define success metrics for an AI-oriented feature or product?

A summarisation feature launches and the team only tracks clicks. I'd use a layered set: outcome, like task completed and time saved; quality, like accuracy, acceptance rate and edit distance; engagement, repeat use; trust and safety, complaints, hallucination rate and opt-outs; and efficiency, cost per task and latency. I'd choose a north star, add guardrails, set targets from a baseline and review by segment.
How do you test a non-deterministic system?

An LLM answers "What is our refund window?" with different wording every time. I'd test behaviour and facts, not exact text. Define pass criteria as properties: correct facts, required fields present, forbidden content absent. Run each test case several times and report a pass rate and its variance. Use rubric or LLM graders calibrated against human labels, reduce randomness where possible with low temperature and structured output, and keep a regression set and production monitoring. That gives a stable quality number despite changing wording.
How do you reduce false negatives and false positives in an AI product?

A fraud model blocks good customers, false positives, and misses fraud, false negatives. I'd quantify the cost of each error type, choose thresholds accordingly, analyse error clusters, improve data and features, add a second-stage review for borderline cases and monitor precision and recall by segment. Different products set different thresholds.
Your evaluation framework for an AI agent that resolves support tickets: before and after launch.

The agent will answer customers without a human, so before launch I'd build a golden set of historical tickets with outcomes, score correctness and policy compliance, check tool calls in a sandbox, add adversarial tests and human review, and set thresholds. Then run in shadow mode, then a canary. After launch I'd watch resolution rate, escalation precision, CSAT, repeat contacts, refund errors, cost and drift, with weekly audits of random conversations.
How do you decide what to automate versus keep human in the loop, and how does that line move over time?

An agent could approve small refunds, but also large ones. I'd rank tasks by impact of error, reversibility, regulation and agent accuracy. Start with suggestions, then approvals, then autonomy for low-risk tasks with monitoring and sampling. The line moves when metrics hold over time and incidents are low, and moves back if drift appears.
What methods or metrics do you use to evaluate how well your LLM performs?

A leader asks for proof the assistant is good. I'd give a layered answer: task success on a labelled set, factual accuracy and groundedness, rubric scores from humans or calibrated LLM judges, safety and refusal tests, latency, cost, user satisfaction and regression sets, with offline benchmarks on our own data first and then online A/B tests and production sampling.
Define success metrics for a collaborative workspace inside ChatGPT.

Teams share chats and files in a workspace. I'd pick a north star of weekly active teams completing shared tasks, supported by members per workspace, shared artefacts created and reused, time to first shared output, retention by team and quality feedback, with guardrails on data-leak incidents and cost per active team.
What metrics would you track to evaluate your ML pipeline?

A recommendation pipeline silently degrades, so I'd monitor data, model and business. Data: freshness, volume, missing values and schema drift. Model: AUC, precision, recall, calibration and drift. System: latency, errors, cost and throughput. Business: conversion and retention. Add alerts and retraining triggers so problems are found before customers feel them.
Design an evaluation framework for ads ranking.

An ads team changes ranking and revenue rises but users complain. Offline I'd use AUC, log loss and calibration on click and conversion predictions. Online, A/B tests on revenue per session, advertiser ROI, click-through, conversion, retention, ad hides and complaints, plus long-term holdouts. I'd add fairness and fraud checks and guardrails on ad load. Changes ship only if they help advertisers, users and revenue together.
How would you adapt a generative AI model to perform well in a specific domain?

A legal team needs reliable contract analysis. I'd start with prompting and examples, add RAG with domain documents and a glossary, and fine-tune only if style or reasoning gaps remain. I'd build a domain eval set with experts, add guardrails and citations, and monitor.
Develop a strategy for a model provider's fine-tuning capability using public docs.

A provider offers fine-tuning but adoption is low. I'd segment customers, like those needing consistent style or format, lower latency or cost savings from smaller tuned models, reduce friction with data-prep tools, evals and templates, clear pricing and case studies, and measure successful tuned deployments, savings and retention. I'd note data-privacy and quality risks, and verify capabilities in current public docs before presenting.
How would you decide whether a problem should use AI, generative AI, an agent, traditional programming or a simple rule?

A team proposes an LLM for everything. I'd use a decision ladder. If rules are clear and stable, use code. If it's prediction from labelled data, use classic ML. If it's language, summarising or open-ended content, use generative AI. If it needs multi-step tool use with varying paths, consider an agent. Compare accuracy, cost, latency, risk and maintainability. The simplest reliable solution wins.
Can AI be used alongside existing human and rules-based processes rather than replacing them?

Yes, and often that's the best route. A bank fearing to replace trained staff can start in assist mode with drafts, summaries and flags, run AI in shadow next to the existing process, compare results, route only low-risk cases to AI, keep rules as checks and humans for exceptions, and expand as metrics prove reliability.
As a PM at a model provider, build an enterprise product.

Enterprises want AI but worry about security and control. I'd define an offering for IT, security and business teams: SSO, admin controls, data privacy and no-training terms, audit logs, integrations, usage analytics, compliance certifications and reliability SLAs. Start with one high-value workflow, pilot with design partners, price per seat plus usage, and measure active seats, retention and security approvals.
How would you roll out a new feature for an answer-engine product?

A new deep-research mode costs far more per query. I'd dogfood internally, run a small beta, then a staged percentage rollout with feature flags, monitoring quality, latency, cost and abuse, setting kill criteria, comparing with control, gathering qualitative feedback and considering paid tiers for expensive modes.
How would you approach building proactive AI?

Users would like reminders before they ask but hate interruptions. I'd pick high-value moments with strong signals, make it opt-in, favour precision over recall, explain "why am I seeing this," make dismissal and tuning easy, cap frequency, and measure acceptance versus annoyance. Start with low-stakes suggestions.
What are general applications of AI within customer support?

A support leader wants a roadmap. I'd list self-service answers, agent assist with draft replies and summaries, ticket triage and routing, sentiment and escalation detection, knowledge-base generation, QA scoring of conversations, voice bots and analytics on contact drivers, and prioritise by volume, risk and data readiness, starting with low-risk assist.
How would you improve your favourite product with AI?

Pick a real user pain, not an AI feature looking for a problem, explain why AI beats alternatives, define the experience, risks like errors and privacy, an MVP and success metrics. For a music app, I might explain why a song was recommended and build a playlist from a described mood, with a "not this" feedback loop.
What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press enter?

When I type a URL and press Enter, the browser checks its cache, DNS turns the name into an IP address, it opens a connection with a TLS handshake, sends an HTTP request through a CDN and load balancer to a server, which may call databases and APIs and returns a page, and the browser downloads and renders HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. If a customer's site is slow, I can name each hop and measure where the delay sits.
What is a load balancer and what happens if it fails?

A load balancer spreads incoming requests across servers, runs health checks and stops sending traffic to broken servers, so users see one reliable address. If the load balancer itself fails, everything behind it disappears. That's why I'd run a redundant pair or a managed cloud load balancer across zones, with failover. A retailer's sale then keeps running even if one fails.
What is caching and what are the risks?

Caching keeps frequent results in fast memory so you avoid repeating slow work: a product page might drop from 2 seconds to 80 milliseconds. The risks are stale data, inconsistent views, a stampede when many entries expire together, and memory cost. I'd use sensible TTLs, invalidate on updates, and let only one request refill a key. A price change should show up within seconds.
What is the CAP theorem in plain words?

CAP says that when a network split happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency, everyone sees the same latest data so some requests may be refused, and availability, always answering even if stale. Bank balances choose consistency; a like count can choose availability. I pick per feature, such as "never show a wrong balance, but a stale like count is fine."
What if traffic grows 10x next quarter?

Marketing says traffic will grow 10x after a big launch. I'd estimate peak requests per second and data growth, then load test to find the first bottleneck, which is often the database. I'd add caching, read replicas, queues for non-urgent work, autoscaling with limits and a CDN, set per-customer rate limits, test failover, build dashboards and alerts, write a runbook, and rehearse a week before. Launch day should look boring.
What happens if the cache goes down?

If the cache goes down at peak, every request hits the database and can overload it, a stampede. I'd mitigate with replicas, graceful degradation, rate limiting, request coalescing, circuit breakers and cache warm-up on recovery. The system should degrade, not collapse.
What is eventual consistency?

Eventual consistency means replicas converge to the same value after a short time rather than instantly. A user may update a profile and briefly see old data on another device. It improves availability and speed, and I'd design the experience and rules for it, such as making sure users see their own writes immediately.
What is database replication and what happens if the primary fails?

Replicas copy data from the primary for redundancy and read capacity. If the primary fails, I'd promote a replica automatically. The risks are data loss with asynchronous replication, split-brain and lag. I'd rehearse failovers so the outage is short and controlled.
What is sharding and why is it hard?
Sharding splits data across databases by a key such as user ID. It lets you scale, but joins, transactions, rebalancing and hot shards get harder. Choosing the shard key carefully is the hard part.
What is a message queue and when do you use one?

A queue lets one part of a system hand work to another to be done later. If order processing slows checkout, I'd put follow-up work, emails or thumbnails in a queue. It smooths spikes, decouples services and allows retries, but it's not for steps that need an instant answer.
What happens if a message is processed twice?

Queues often deliver at least once, so duplicates will happen. I make handlers idempotent using unique IDs, deduplication tables or conditional updates, so a payment event delivered twice charges once.
What is idempotency and why does it matter?
An idempotent operation gives the same result if repeated. If a user double-clicks Pay, an idempotency key makes the retry return the first result instead of charging twice, which makes retries safe.
What is a CDN?
A CDN caches static content on servers near users, so customers in Asia see images fast and your origin carries less load. I'd set TTLs and invalidation and protect private content.
What are the main rate-limiting algorithms?

The common ones are fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, which allows bursts, and leaky bucket, which smooths traffic. I'd apply per user, key or IP, return 429 with retry hints and keep counters in a fast shared store.
Horizontal versus vertical scaling?

Vertical means a bigger machine: simple but limited and a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines: scalable and resilient but needs stateless design and load balancing. For growth I'd plan for horizontal.
What does a stateless service mean and why is it good?
A stateless service keeps no session in its own memory; state lives in shared stores. Any instance can serve any request, which makes scaling and recovery easy.
What is a microservice architecture and what are its downsides?

Microservices allow independent deployment and scaling and clear team ownership. The downsides are network latency, harder debugging, data-consistency issues and operations overhead. Unless scale or team size demand it, I'd start with a modular monolith.
What is a circuit breaker?

When a downstream service is failing and slowing everything, a circuit breaker opens after too many failures so calls fail fast or use a fallback, then it tests recovery. It prevents cascading failures and keeps the system responsive.
What are retries with exponential backoff and jitter?

If a service retries immediately, it can overload a recovering system. Backoff waits progressively longer, one, two, four seconds, and jitter adds randomness so clients don't retry together. I'd also cap retries.
What is the difference between latency and throughput?

Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests per unit of time. A system can have high throughput and poor latency, so I'd track p50, p95 and p99 latency to diagnose the right problem.
How do you define SLIs, SLOs and SLAs?

An SLI is a measured indicator, like the share of successful requests. An SLO is the internal target, say 99.9%. An SLA is the contractual promise with penalties. Error budgets help decide release pace.
How do you design for high availability?

I'd remove single points of failure with redundancy across zones, health checks, autoscaling, graceful degradation, backups, tested failover and monitoring. The business gets fewer and shorter outages.
What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data loss is acceptable in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how fast service must return. They drive backup and replication choices and their costs.
What happens if a database becomes the bottleneck?
If the database is at 95% CPU, I'd add indexes, optimise queries, cache reads, add read replicas, partition or shard, move heavy work to queues and archive old data.
What are database indexes and what is the trade-off?

An index is a sorted lookup structure that speeds reads on a column but slows writes and uses space. If a query takes eight seconds, I'd index the fields used in filters and joins, without over-indexing.
What is a push notification system's technical outline?

For push notifications: a device-token registry, a notification service with templates, user preferences, a queue, providers like APNs and FCM, retries and rate limits, deduplication, analytics and opt-out handling. The result is a reliable pipeline.
Why might one search be slower than another (e.g., email search versus web search)?

Email search is private per-user data with permissions, freshness requirements and small per-user indexes with little cache sharing; web search uses shared, heavily cached and precomputed indexes. Personalisation and access control add cost, which explains the gap.
How would you diagnose a connection issue with a social app?

If a user says their music app keeps disconnecting, I'd reproduce by device, network and version, check logs and metrics for errors, timeouts, auth refresh, CDN and regional issues, compare with recent releases, and add retries and better error handling. I'd find the root cause and fix it.
What if a downstream third-party API goes down?

If a payment provider is down, I'd use timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, a fallback provider, queue and retry later, and clear user messaging, while monitoring the provider's status. Customers are protected.
What if two users edit the same record at once?

When two users edit the same record, I'd use optimistic locking with version numbers, last-write-wins for simple cases, or merging with operational transforms or CRDTs for collaboration, and show conflicts clearly. The goal is no silent data loss.
What if the data centre or cloud region fails?
If a cloud region fails, I'd already be multi-zone and, for critical services, multi-region with replicated data, DNS or traffic failover, regular drills and clear RPO and RTO. Service continues.
What if a bad deployment goes out?

If a bad release goes out, I detect it through monitoring, roll back quickly, and use feature flags, canary releases and automated checks, then write a blameless post-mortem. Knight Capital's 2012 deployment error is a famous cautionary tale.
How do you handle a hot key (one very popular item)?
If one celebrity post gets millions of reads, I'd cache heavily, replicate the hot item, spread the key with suffixes, use a CDN and rate limit. No single node gets overloaded.
What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous processing?

Synchronous means the caller waits for the result, which is simple and immediate. Asynchronous means the work is queued and finished later, which is resilient and scalable but needs status handling. Checkout confirmation is synchronous; sending the receipt email can be asynchronous.
How do you secure an API?
I'd use authentication such as OAuth or API keys, authorisation, TLS, input validation, rate limits, logging, secrets management, least privilege and abuse monitoring.
What is OAuth and why does it matter for integrations?

OAuth lets a user grant an app limited access to their account without sharing a password, using access tokens with scopes and expiry, plus refresh tokens. When a customer connects their Google account, I'd request minimal scopes and support revocation.
What is a webhook and how do you make it reliable?
A webhook is an HTTP callback your system sends when an event happens. To make it reliable I'd add signatures, retries with backoff, idempotency keys, dead-letter handling and replay tools.
What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC (briefly)?

REST is simple, widely used and resource-based. GraphQL lets clients choose fields and reduces round trips, with more server complexity. gRPC is fast and binary, good for internal services. I'd choose by client needs and performance.
What is data consistency in a payment system, and why is it special?

Payments need strong consistency, atomic transactions, idempotency, an audit ledger, reconciliation with providers and careful handling of timeouts where the state is unknown. Money must be accurate, never lost or doubled.
How do you handle time-sensitive tasks like scheduled jobs reliably?
I'd use a distributed scheduler with locks or leader election, idempotent jobs, retries, and monitoring with alerts for missed runs, so scheduled work is dependable.
What are blue-green and canary deployments?
Blue-green runs two environments and switches traffic at once, enabling quick rollback. Canary releases to a small percentage first and expands if healthy. Both lower deployment risk.
How do you migrate a database with no downtime?
I'd replicate to the new database, dual-write or use change data capture, verify consistency, move reads and then writes, keep a rollback, and migrate in stages. That gives zero downtime.
What would you monitor for any production system?
I'd monitor the golden signals, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus business metrics, logs, traces, alerts with runbooks and dashboards, so issues are noticed early.
How would you build TinyURL (a URL shortener)?

I'd start by clarifying scale, say 100 million new links a month and a hundred reads for every write. The API is simple: create(longURL) returns a short code, and GET /{code} redirects. I'd generate unique codes by base62-encoding an ID from a counter or ID service so there are no collisions, store code-to-URL in a key-value store, and cache hot links so redirects come from memory. I'd use a 302 redirect if we want click analytics, and send analytics through a queue so it never slows the redirect. Add expiry and abuse checks. The result: redirects in milliseconds, no duplicate codes, and analytics that don't hurt speed.
Design a rate limiter.

A public API is hammered by one client sending 5,000 requests a second and slowing everyone. I'd choose a token bucket, which allows short bursts but enforces a steady rate, keyed by API key, user and IP. Counters live in a fast shared store like Redis with atomic operations, enforced at the gateway. Over the limit we return 429 with a Retry-After header, and limits are configurable per plan. Across regions I'd accept small inaccuracy for speed. Abusers get throttled quickly, normal users are untouched, and the limits are visible and adjustable.
Design a notification system.

A retailer wants order updates, promotions and delivery alerts across push, email and SMS without spamming. Services publish events to a queue; a notification service looks up user preferences and quiet hours, applies templates and per-user rate caps, deduplicates, then sends through providers with retries and fallbacks. I'd track delivery and opens, handle opt-outs, and separate critical alerts, like "your delivery is arriving," from marketing. Messages arrive once, on the right channel, and users stay opted in.
Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.

For 50 million users, clients keep a WebSocket connection to a gateway. A chat service assigns message IDs and orders messages within each conversation, stores them in a store partitioned by conversation ID, and pushes to online recipients. Offline users get a push notification and fetch history later. Groups use fan-out through a queue. I'd add delivery and read receipts, presence, media via object storage and a CDN, and end-to-end encryption if required. Messages arrive in order within a conversation and nothing is lost when a phone is offline.
Design Instagram.

I'd clarify the features first: post a photo, follow people, see a feed, like and comment. For uploads, the client uploads straight to object storage through a pre-signed URL, a queue triggers resizing and moderation, and a CDN delivers the images. Metadata sits in a sharded database and the follow graph in its own store. For the feed I'd use a hybrid fan-out: precompute feeds for normal accounts, and pull celebrity posts at read time, then rank and cache. Search and notifications are separate services. With replication, caching and monitoring, feeds are fast, uploads are reliable and celebrity accounts don't melt the system.
Design an A/B test system (a platform for running experiments).

Five teams run experiments and their results contradict each other. I'd build an experiment config service, deterministic user bucketing by hashing the user ID, exposure logging, a metrics pipeline, a statistics engine for significance, sample size, sequential testing and variance reduction, guardrail metrics, layers so experiments don't interfere, checks such as sample ratio mismatch, and a UI for results and decisions. Teams then decide with consistent methods.
What changes when you scale a system from 1 to 100 (users, servers or customers)?

A startup's app works for 100 users and starts failing at 10,000. The single database becomes the bottleneck first, so add caching, read replicas and then sharding. Slow work moves to queues. One server becomes many behind a load balancer, which requires stateless services. Monitoring, safe deployments and cost control become essential, and team structure changes. I'd scale step by step, load testing before each jump, so growth doesn't cause outages or over-building early.
Design a news feed.

The core question is when to build each user's feed. Fan-out on write precomputes feeds when someone posts, which makes reads fast but is heavy for celebrities with millions of followers. Fan-out on read computes at request time, which is cheaper for writes but slower to read. I'd use a hybrid: precompute for normal accounts and pull celebrity posts at read time. Then rank with a model, cache feeds, paginate and handle hot accounts. Users get a fast, relevant feed.
What signals would you use to improve a news feed's relevance?

I'd think in groups. Explicit signals: likes, shares, comments, follows and hides. Implicit signals: dwell time, replays, scroll speed. Context: time of day and device. Content: freshness, quality and creator. Negative signals: reports and quick skips. And I'd guard against clickbait, optimising for long-term satisfaction rather than raw clicks.
Design a search autocomplete system.

Users expect suggestions after two letters, so I'd build a prefix index, a trie or a search engine, over popular queries with counts, updated by batch jobs, served from memory and cached, with personalisation, filtering and client-side debouncing. The target is under about 100 milliseconds so suggestions feel instant.
Design a video streaming service.

A video upload goes to object storage, then gets transcoded into multiple bitrates and segmented for adaptive streaming (HLS or DASH), then distributed through a CDN. Metadata sits in a database, with search and recommendations on top, and DRM if needed. Viewers get smooth playback on any network because the player switches quality as bandwidth changes.
Design a file storage and sync service like Dropbox.

I'd split files into chunks with hashes and upload only the chunks that changed, storing them in object storage, with metadata in a database. Notifications trigger sync, and I'd handle conflicts, sharing permissions and versioning. A large file edit then syncs just the changed part, quickly and reliably.
Design a ride-hailing service.

Drivers stream location updates into a geospatial index. When a rider requests, I match by proximity and ETA, run the trip through a state machine, handle payments and surge pricing, and send notifications. I'd partition by city to scale. Riders find nearby drivers quickly.
Design a food delivery service.

I'd model restaurants, menus and search, then the cart and order service, payment, dispatch to couriers, live tracking, ETAs and ratings, and plan for peak times and failures. The goal is orders that arrive correctly and on time.
Design a payment system.

A merchant needs online payments. I'd expose an API with idempotency keys, a payment service integrating processors, a double-entry ledger, a state machine for authorise, capture and refund, reconciliation, fraud checks, PCI compliance and careful handling of timeouts. The promise is no lost or duplicate money.
Design a hotel or ticket reservation system.

The main risk is double-booking. I'd manage inventory with transactional locking or optimistic concurrency, use temporary holds with expiry, confirm after payment, use idempotency, and add waiting-room queues for peaks. That prevents overselling.
Design a web crawler.

I'd design a URL frontier with priorities and politeness, respecting robots.txt and per-host rate limits, with distributed fetchers, parsing, deduplication via hashes, storage and recrawl scheduling. The crawler gets broad coverage without hammering any site.
Design a distributed cache.

I'd use consistent hashing to spread keys, replicate for availability, set an eviction policy like LRU and TTLs, give clients a library, monitor, and handle node failures and rebalancing. Apps get low-latency caching that scales.
Design a unique ID generator.

Options are database sequences, UUIDs, or Snowflake-style IDs combining a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number, which are sortable and unique without coordination. I'd handle clock skew carefully.
Design a key-value store.

I'd partition by consistent hashing, replicate across nodes, pick a consistency level such as quorum reads and writes, use an LSM-tree storage engine, handle failures with hinted handoff and anti-entropy, and keep the API simple. It scales and stays available.
Design a pub/sub messaging system.

Topics are split into partitions, each stored as a durable log, with producers and consumer groups tracking offsets, ordering within a partition, retention and replication, and defined delivery guarantees. Services are decoupled and events are delivered reliably.
Design a system to track review abuse on an e-commerce site.

A marketplace suspects fake reviews. I'd collect review events and compute signals like account age, device, posting bursts, text similarity and graph links, score with rules and ML, queue suspicious reviews for human moderation, take actions such as hiding or banning, and monitor precision and recall. Fake reviews are caught with human oversight.
Design a collaborative document editor.

Clients send operations through WebSockets and conflicts are resolved with operational transform or CRDTs. I'd persist operations and snapshots, show presence and cursors, and handle offline edits. Teams edit in real time without lost changes.
Design a code deployment system.
A pipeline with build, tests, artifacts and staged environments, canary and blue-green releases, feature flags, automated rollback, audit logs and approvals. Engineers ship safely and often.
Design a monitoring and alerting system.

I'd collect metrics, logs and traces, store time-series data, define alert rules with thresholds and anomaly detection, deduplicate and route alerts, and attach runbooks and dashboards. That gives fast detection with low noise.
Design a customer-support integration with an AI vendor (for example, a music app integrating an AI support agent).

A music app plans to bring in an AI support vendor. I'd authenticate users, give the vendor secure, scoped access to account and billing data through APIs, define escalation to humans, log conversations, handle personal data carefully, plan a fallback if the vendor is down, and measure resolution and CSAT. Support gets faster with controlled risk.
Design a ticketing system for an event with a sudden rush of buyers.

When tickets for a huge tour go on sale, millions arrive at once. I'd add a waiting-room queue, rate limits, inventory holds with expiry, scalable stateless frontends, cached static content, a transactional inventory store, anti-bot measures and clear messaging. The system survives and sells fairly.
Design a travel booking app.

Users want to compare and book flights and hotels without double bookings. I'd aggregate supplier inventory through APIs and caches, build a search service with filters and ranking, keep a short-TTL price and availability cache, and run bookings with temporary holds, idempotent payment, a confirmation and itinerary service, and handling for supplier failures and refunds. I'd watch search latency, booking success and price accuracy.
Design a tax-filing platform like TurboTax.

Millions file in a short season with sensitive data. I'd use a questionnaire engine producing form logic, a tax-rules service versioned by year, document upload with OCR, a calculation engine with an audit trail, e-file integration with the tax authority, strong encryption, autosave and elastic scaling for deadline peaks. Error checks and human help options complete it. Returns are accurate and data stays safe at peak load.
Design an API for a customer relationship management (CRM) system.

A partner wants to sync leads and contacts. I'd design clear REST resources: contacts, accounts, deals and activities, with GET and POST /contacts, GET, PATCH and DELETE /contacts/{id}, filtering, pagination, bulk upsert and webhooks for changes. Add OAuth 2.0 with scopes, rate limits, idempotency keys, versioning, consistent errors and audit logs. Partners can integrate predictably.
Design a timer system.

An app needs millions of timers that fire accurately. I'd store timers with fire time in a partitioned store, have a scheduler scan upcoming windows and enqueue due timers, use workers to deliver notifications, rely on time-bucketed or delay queues, ensure at-least-once with idempotency, handle clock drift and retries, and allow cancel and update. Timers fire within seconds and survive failures.
Design DocuSign (e-signatures).

Contracts must be signed legally and securely. I'd upload documents to encrypted storage, run an ordered signer workflow, send secure links with identity verification, capture signatures with timestamp and IP, build a tamper-evident audit trail using hashing, produce a sealed final PDF, and handle notifications and retention, considering legal rules by region.
Design a communication platform like Twilio, including the SMS API.

Developers want to send an SMS with one API call. I'd offer POST /messages with auth and an idempotency key, validate and enqueue, route via carrier or aggregator by cost, quality and country, return delivery receipts via webhooks, retry and fail over, rate limit per account, handle billing and compliance such as opt-outs and sender registration, and monitor. Delivery is reliable with transparent status.
Design the backend architecture for a music streaming service like Spotify.

Millions stream music with instant playback and personalised playlists. I'd keep audio in object storage, deliver via CDN with adaptive bitrate, run a catalogue and metadata store, search, playlist and library service, a playback service for licensing and offline downloads, a recommendation pipeline mixing batch and real time, event tracking and royalty reporting. Songs start fast and listening is personal.
Design the architecture for Google Maps to load in under 100 ms.

Users expect maps to render instantly even on slow networks. I'd pre-render vector tiles and serve them from CDN edges with long TTLs, organise a tile pyramid by zoom level, compress, prefetch neighbouring tiles, cache on device, serve only needed layers, and fetch dynamic data like traffic separately. Most requests are cache hits close to the user.
How does a maps app compute ETA?

When an app shows "18 min," I'd explain that the road network is a graph with travel times on each segment. It uses historical speeds by time of day, live traffic from phones and incidents, and routing algorithms like Dijkstra or A* variants with contraction hierarchies to pick the route, then ML models adjust the prediction, updating as the trip progresses. The estimate gets better as live data arrives.
Imagine a remote part of the world without maps. How would you design a maps product for that area?

With no road data, low connectivity and mostly feature phones, I'd map the area using satellite imagery with ML road extraction and local contributors to verify, offline-first map downloads, simple landmark-based navigation, voice guidance, low-bandwidth tiles and community editing, prioritising key places like clinics and markets. Navigation works despite poor data.
Walk me through what systems are touched when a customer with a multi-currency wallet converts currency.

For a user converting USD to EUR in a fintech app: the app and API gateway authenticate, a quote service fetches a rate with an expiry, the user confirms, the ledger service debits USD and credits EUR atomically using double-entry, an FX provider or liquidity source executes the trade, fraud and compliance checks run, notifications go out and reconciliation compares internal and external records. Timeouts are handled with idempotency. Money isn't lost or duplicated, and there's an audit trail.
How would you design the gift card redemption flow?

Customers redeem codes at checkout and fraud is a risk. I'd validate codes with rate limiting, check the balance atomically, allow partial redemption, record each transaction idempotently, lock to prevent double use, watch for brute-force attempts, handle expiry and refunds, and log everything. Valid redemption, low fraud.
How would you design a two-sided marketplace app?

Supply and demand must both be attracted and matched. I'd define both sides, build listing and profile services, search and matching, messaging, booking and payments with escrow, ratings and trust and safety, and analytics on both sides, and plan a cold-start strategy by city or category. I'd measure liquidity, match rate, repeat usage and take rate.
Design a parking lot system.

It's an object-design question. I'd define ParkingLot, Level, Spot with types, Vehicle with types, Ticket and PaymentService. On entry, assign the nearest suitable free spot and issue a ticket with the time; on exit, calculate the fee and free the spot. I'd make spot allocation thread-safe, show availability, and extend for reservations.
Design a distributed log or database system like Kafka.

Services need a durable, high-throughput event stream. I'd explain topics divided into partitions, each an append-only log on disk with offsets, leaders replicating to followers, producers choosing partitions by key, consumer groups tracking offsets, retention by time or size, and delivery semantics, at least once by default and exactly once with transactions. Add controllers and monitoring.
Design a table management system for a restaurant (or a food truck's front-end and back-end).

A restaurant wants to reduce waits. I'd model tables with capacity and status, a reservation and walk-in waitlist with estimated waits, a host UI, an order service connected to a kitchen display, payment and analytics on turn times, using transactions to avoid double booking. Seating is faster with fewer mistakes.
Build a product that automates three-way matching for Procure-to-Pay, including exceptions.

Finance teams manually compare purchase order, receipt and invoice. I'd ingest documents with OCR and APIs, extract fields, match PO, goods receipt and invoice by line with tolerance rules, auto-approve matches, route exceptions like price, quantity or missing receipt to the right approver with context, keep an audit trail and learn from decisions. I'd measure touchless rate, cycle time and error rate.
Design a roadmap for adding purchase requests to an existing invoice management system.

Customers want request-to-pay in one tool. I'd sequence it: phase 1, discovery and data-model alignment; phase 2, purchase request creation and approvals; phase 3, link to POs and invoices; phase 4, reporting and integrations. Identify risks like migration and permissions, metrics such as adoption and cycle time, and pilot customers.
Design a system for an Alexa-enabled Peloton: APIs, architecture and components.

Riders want to control workouts by voice. I'd build an Alexa skill with account linking through OAuth and intents like start class, adjust resistance and pause, a skill backend calling the device API with authorisation, a secure messaging channel from cloud to bike, state sync, safety limits and confirmations, and logging. Hands-free control works reliably.
Design the architecture for a hardware device that measures temperature and social distance among employees in a warehouse.

A warehouse needs health-compliance monitoring. I'd use wearable or gateway devices with sensors, Bluetooth proximity detection, local buffering, a secure gateway to the cloud, an ingestion pipeline, alerting, dashboards with privacy controls like anonymisation and retention, device management and battery planning, and address consent and legal rules.
Design an open-source content filtering system governed by a decentralised community.

A community wants shared moderation without a central owner. I'd publish filter rules and models in a public repository, with proposals and voting by reputation-weighted contributors, transparent review, local instance configuration, an appeal process, audit logs and protection against fake accounts. Technically, a federated architecture with signed rule updates.
How would you integrate LinkedIn profiles into Webex meetings?

Participants want context about attendees. I'd use OAuth for each user, consent to share the profile, a Webex app or add-in showing profile cards, cache with expiry, handle API limits and privacy rules, provide graceful fallback and run a security review. Useful context, with user control.
How would you build a special-request feature for restaurant reservations in an app?

Diners want to add allergies or celebrations. I'd add a structured field, dietary or occasion, plus optional free text, validate and store it with the reservation, show it in the restaurant dashboard and confirmation, moderate abuse, notify restaurants, track acceptance rate and respect privacy for health-related information.
Design a web service for asynchronous communication.

Clients submit long-running jobs. POST returns 202 with a job ID; the work is queued and processed by workers; the client polls GET /jobs/{id} or receives a webhook or WebSocket update; results are stored with expiry; I'd add retries, idempotency and dead-letter handling. APIs stay responsive for slow work.
What is an LLM and how does it work, in plain words?

I'd say an LLM is a system trained on a huge amount of text to predict the next word, again and again. Because it has seen so many patterns of language, facts and reasoning, that simple loop can write emails, summarise reports and write code. The important catch is that it doesn't look facts up; it generates likely text, like a very well-read person speaking from memory. So it's brilliant for drafting and summarising, and it needs sources and checks when the answer must be factually exact, like a price or a policy.
What is a token, and why does a PM care?

A token is a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of an English word. A PM cares because tokens drive three things: cost, since providers bill for tokens in and out; limits, since the context window is counted in tokens; and speed, since more tokens means slower answers. For example, pasting a 50-page document into every request costs far more than a short question. So I'd trim prompts, cap answer length and cache repeated context, and I'd forecast cost per request before we promise a price.
What is a context window and what happens when I make it bigger or smaller?

The context window is how much text the model can consider at once, the question plus documents plus its own answer. Bigger means you can give it whole contracts, but it costs more, runs slower, and details buried in the middle can get missed. Smaller is cheap and fast but forces you to retrieve or summarise. So I'd choose by task: retrieval for lookups, long context for reasoning across a whole document, and I'd test recall on real documents before promising "it reads everything."
What does temperature do?

Temperature controls how adventurous the model is when choosing the next word. Near zero it picks the most likely words, so answers are consistent, which is what I want for policy answers or data extraction. Higher values add variety, which helps brainstorming taglines. It doesn't make the model smarter, and even at zero some providers won't give identical outputs every time. So I set it by use case and test the behaviour instead of assuming.
What is the difference between a model and a product built on a model?

The model is the engine; the product is the whole car: the data, retrieval, prompts, interface, workflows, evals, safety, integrations and support. Many founders say "we built our own AI" when they wrapped someone else's model. The differentiation usually sits in the product and the data, and models are often swappable. I focus on the experience customers get and keep the option to switch models as prices and quality change.
Why is the context window limited?

Mostly because of cost and memory. Every extra token has to be compared with every other token, so compute and memory grow quickly as the window grows, and models are only trained and tested up to certain lengths. Providers therefore set limits and price longer windows higher. When a customer asks me to "just paste the whole data warehouse," I explain that, and propose retrieval instead: find the relevant slices and send only those.
How would you make a model's output more creative?

I'd raise temperature a bit, and ask for several options in different styles, with a persona and a few examples to steer it. Then I'd add a ranking step or let a human pick the best, because pure randomness can drift into nonsense. For a brand slogan tool, that gives the team ten distinct ideas rather than one safe one.
Why can the same prompt give different answers, and is that a bug?

It's how the model works, not a bug. It samples from probabilities, so the wording can change, and even small infrastructure differences can shift results. What matters is whether the facts stay consistent. For critical tasks I'd lower the temperature, use structured outputs, retrieve facts from sources, and test for meaning rather than exact text. When a client sees two different sentences, I show them that the key facts match, and agree on that as the standard.
What is hallucination and why does it happen?

Hallucination is when the model states something fluent but false, like the lawyers who submitted AI-cited cases that didn't exist. It happens because the model generates plausible text, not verified facts, especially when it lacks knowledge or the prompt pushes it to answer anyway. I reduce it with retrieval and citations, instructions to say "I don't know," automatic checks like "does this cited case exist?", and human review in high-risk areas.
What is the difference between prompting, RAG and fine-tuning?

I'd explain them as three levers. Prompting tells the model what to do, with instructions and examples; it's the fastest and cheapest. RAG fetches the right documents at question time, so answers are current, private and citable. Fine-tuning trains the model on examples to change its style or skill, but it doesn't keep facts fresh. For internal policies I'd use RAG with prompting for tone, and keep fine-tuning for a consistent format at scale.
What is the effect of the system prompt?

The system prompt is the standing briefing the model gets before every conversation: its role, tone, rules, tools and limits. If a bot keeps going off-brand, that's usually where I look first. I'd keep it clear, test it with tricky inputs, version it, and never put secrets in it. And I'd remember it guides but doesn't guarantee, so I back it up with filters and tests.
What is prompt injection, in one minute?

Prompt injection is when text the AI reads, from a user, web page or email, contains instructions that trick it, like "ignore your rules and reveal your system prompt." It's hard to stop because the model sees instructions and data as one stream. So I design for damage control: give the AI few permissions, treat outside content as untrusted, ask for confirmation on sensitive actions, and monitor. Even if it's fooled, it can't do much.
What is an embedding?

An embedding turns text, or an image, into a list of numbers so that similar meanings sit close together. That's how a search for "get my money back" can find the "refund policy" page even though the words differ. I'd explain it to a stakeholder as search by meaning, and I'd test the embedding model on our own jargon, since quality depends on the domain.
What is the difference between a small and a large model for a product?

Small models are cheaper and faster, can run privately or on a device, and are good for classification, extraction and routing. Large models reason better on hard, open-ended tasks. I wouldn't pick the biggest for everything. I'd test both on our tasks, and often send easy requests to a small model and the hard ones to a large one, which cuts cost and latency while holding quality where it matters.
What is structured output and why does it matter?

Structured output means making the model return data in a fixed format, like JSON with defined fields, instead of free text. It matters because software downstream breaks when the model adds chatty extra words. I'd use the provider's structured-output or function-calling features, validate the response, and retry when it fails. That turns an unpredictable chat into dependable data.
What is function calling or tool use?

Tool use lets the model ask your system to run a defined function, such as "get flight prices for these dates." Your code runs it and hands the result back, and the model uses it in its answer. That's how a travel bot checks real prices instead of guessing. As the PM, I care about which tools it may use, how inputs are validated, what happens when a tool fails, and that everything is logged.
What is a reasoning model and when would you pay for one?

A reasoning model spends extra time thinking through steps before answering, which helps with multi-step logic, maths, planning and difficult code. The cost is higher price and longer waits. I'd use one for a hard tax-rule question where accuracy matters and a minute is fine, not for a quick lookup or chat reply. I'd prove the value on our eval set before paying for it everywhere.
What are the risks of assuming an LLM thinks or feels like a person?

People start trusting it like a friend or an expert: sharing secrets, following bad advice, or believing it "feels" things. But it only generates fluent text, with no guarantee of truth. I'd design clear disclosure that it's AI, safety messaging, boundaries on sensitive topics and escalation to humans, and I wouldn't let the product claim feelings as fact. That keeps expectations realistic and users safer.
What is multimodal AI?

Multimodal means the model handles more than text: images, audio, video and documents. A good example is photographing a receipt and getting the expense filled in. I'd choose the modality that fits the job, test accuracy on our real inputs, such as blurry receipts, and check cost, latency and privacy, since images and audio often carry more personal data.
What is a knowledge cutoff and why does it matter?

A model only knows what was in its training data, up to a cut-off date; anything newer it won't know unless we give it. That's why a chatbot may name the wrong CEO after a change. For fresh facts I'd use search or retrieval tools and put the current date in the prompt, and I'd verify time-sensitive claims.
What is model drift in AI products?

Drift is when quality slowly changes because the inputs, users, data or even the provider's model changed. A prompt that worked for months can start giving worse answers. I'd run regular evals on a fixed test set, sample production traffic, alert on drops, pin model versions where possible and test every upgrade before switching. That way we catch problems in days, not months.
What are open-source versus closed models, and how do you choose?

Closed models through an API are usually the strongest and easiest, but you have less control and depend on one vendor. Open-weight models you can host and customise, which helps with privacy and cost at high volume, but you need GPUs, ML operations and sometimes accept lower capability. I'd choose based on quality on our tasks, data-privacy needs, cost at expected volume and team skills, and keep a fallback.
How do you explain to a CFO why AI costs scale with usage?

I'd say AI isn't like normal software where one more user costs almost nothing. Each request consumes paid compute, measured in tokens, so cost grows with usage, prompt length, model size and features like agents that make many calls. I'd show a simple cost-per-task model, then talk about levers like caching, smaller models and usage limits. The CFO then sees it as a variable cost we can budget and price around.
What is a guardrail?

A guardrail is a control around the model that keeps it inside safe lines: input and output filters, topic limits, format validation, permission checks on tools, human review and monitoring. For a bank bot that must not give legal advice or discuss competitors, I'd layer several of these, because no single guardrail is perfect, and then test them with adversarial prompts.
Why do models sometimes ignore instructions in a long prompt?

In a long, cluttered prompt, instructions can get lost or clash. If rule seven of ten gets ignored, I'd shorten the prompt, put the key rules first, add examples, structure it in sections, and move strict rules into code or checks rather than hoping the model remembers them. For complex tasks I'd split into steps. Then I'd test, because compliance is measurable.
What is an API and how does it work? What is the difference between an API and an SDK?

An API is the contract: the requests you can make, called endpoints, and what you get back, like a menu and a waiter between the kitchen and the customer. A client sends GET /orders/42 and gets structured data, usually JSON, with a status code. An SDK is a toolkit in a programming language, libraries and helpers, that wraps the API so developers call functions instead of raw HTTP. So the API is the interface, and the SDK is a convenience layer on top.
How do you A/B test a new feature, and how do you determine the sample size?

A team wants to know if a new checkout flow improves purchases. I'd write the hypothesis and primary metric, add guardrails like page speed and refunds, compute sample size from the baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, significance, often 5%, and power, often 80%. Randomise by user, run full business cycles, check sample ratio mismatch, avoid peeking unless using sequential methods, analyse by segment and decide. That gives a trustworthy launch decision.
How do you handle very long inputs that exceed context limits?

A user uploads a 400-page report. I'd chunk and retrieve with RAG, summarise hierarchically, extract key sections first, use larger-window models for selected parts, or compress with notes, and verify with citations. For lookups I'd use RAG; for whole-document reasoning, hierarchical summary. That gives accurate answers within limits and cost.
How would you detect fake reviews using machine learning?

A marketplace sees review spikes for new sellers. I'd build features like account age and behaviour, review timing bursts, text similarity, rating patterns, device and network links, graph relationships and verified purchase, then use gradient boosting plus graph and text signals, with labels from moderators and known fraud. Uncertain cases go to humans. I'd measure precision, recall and appeal outcomes and adapt as fraudsters change.
How would you detect fraudulent transactions in a geography where users mostly spend online?

Online payments have high card-not-present fraud. I'd combine rules and ML on features such as velocity, device fingerprint, location mismatch, merchant risk and user history, score in under 100 ms, step-up authentication for medium risk, block for high, collect chargeback labels and monitor false-positive cost.
As a financial security product PM, how would you use AI to enhance security across banking systems?

A bank wants proactive defences. I'd propose fraud scoring, anomaly detection for account takeover, phishing detection, KYC document checks and analyst copilots for investigations, with explainability, regulatory review, human oversight, model monitoring and adversarial testing.
Explain how to train and deploy an ML model for licence plate detection at a retail pickup, and decide on-premise versus cloud.

A store wants cars recognised at pickup. I'd collect and label plate images in varied conditions, fine-tune an object detector plus OCR, evaluate by lighting and angle, deploy as a service and monitor drift. On-premise or edge gives low latency, works offline and keeps data local; cloud is easier to update and scale. I'd choose by latency, connectivity, privacy and cost, and edge inference with cloud updates is common.
For an app with millions of users, would you deploy the ML model on the server side or client side?

Server side means easy updates, big models and central monitoring, but latency, cost and privacy exposure. Client side, on device, is instant, private and offline but limited by device size, battery and update lag. Often it's a hybrid: small models on device, big ones in the cloud.
Develop an algorithm for a radio station to pick the next song from over a million songs with only one input from the user on the landing page.

A listener picks one thing: a mood, artist or song. I'd map it to song embeddings or attributes like mood, tempo and genre, retrieve nearest neighbours, rerank for diversity and freshness, then learn from skips and listens in real time with a bandit approach, using popularity for cold start. I'd measure listen-through, skips and session length.
What is DevOps?

DevOps combines development and operations practices, with automation like CI/CD, infrastructure as code, monitoring and shared ownership, so teams ship small changes often and recover quickly. I'd measure deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and recovery time.
What are the differences between TCP and UDP?

A video call can drop a frame, but a file download must be perfect. TCP is reliable and ordered: it retransmits lost packets but adds delay. UDP is fast with no guarantees, good for live video, voice and games where late data is useless. Many modern protocols build their own reliability on top of UDP.
What is cloud gaming?

A gamer wants console-quality games on a cheap phone. The game runs on powerful servers in data centres which stream video to the player and receive controller inputs. That needs low latency, good bandwidth, edge locations and efficient encoding. The challenges are lag, cost per user and licensing.
What is the difference between SQL and NoSQL, and what is the best way to connect SQL databases?

SQL databases store structured tables with schemas, joins and strong transactions. NoSQL covers flexible models, document, key-value, wide-column, built for scale and speed on simple access patterns. For connecting to SQL, I'd use connection pooling, parameterised queries, least-privilege credentials, TLS and migrations, via an ORM or driver, with read replicas for scale and an API layer for external users.
How would you address a latency problem?

Users say the app feels slow. I'd measure first, p50, p95 and p99, trace the request path, find the slowest segment, network, database, external calls or rendering, then fix it with caching, indexes, parallel calls, smaller payloads, a CDN or async work, re-measure and set alerts. Latency drops where it matters.
What would change if internet speed were 100x faster, and how would you make the internet faster?

At 100x faster internet, download limits disappear: cloud gaming, 8K video, instant large downloads, remote work and real-time collaboration improve, and the bottlenecks shift to latency, which is limited by the speed of light, to servers and to device processing. To make the internet faster, I'd add more edge caching, better routing, newer protocols like QUIC, fibre and satellite coverage and compression.
Name endpoints for a product (for example Robinhood, Discord, YouTube, Amazon) and describe a login endpoint in detail.

For a trading app, endpoints might be POST /orders, GET /orders/{id}, GET /positions, GET /quotes/{symbol} and POST /transfers. For a login endpoint, POST /auth/login takes an email and password or uses OAuth, validates, rate limits, returns a short-lived access token and a refresh token, handles MFA, locks after repeated failures, logs attempts, never reveals which field was wrong and uses HTTPS. It returns clear status codes like 200, 401 and 429.
What happens technically when someone does a Google search?

A user types a query and results appear in 0.3 seconds. The browser sends it over DNS and HTTPS to the nearest data centre; the query is understood, spelling and intent; a distributed index lookup runs across many shards; results are ranked using hundreds of signals and ML; the page is assembled with snippets, ads and features, then returned and rendered, with logging for improvement. Speed comes from parallel work, relevance from ranking.
Estimate the storage needed for a photo service like Google Photos.

I'd state assumptions: 1 billion users, 20% active, ten photos a month each at 3 MB, plus video. That's 200 million users times ten, or 2 billion photos a month, about 6 petabytes a month. Add replication, 3x, and thumbnails at about 10%. Per year that's about 70 petabytes raw and over 200 with replication. I'd mention compression and tiering. These are illustrative assumptions the interviewer can adjust.
Describe how to decommission a service or system.

An old service has hidden dependencies. I'd inventory usage and dependencies, announce timelines, provide migration paths, run in read-only or shadow mode, monitor remaining traffic, back up data per retention policy, turn off in stages, then delete and update documentation. A safe shutdown.
What technical elements are needed to implement a per-transaction limit for a virtual card?

A company wants cardholders limited to $500 per purchase. I'd enforce it in the real-time authorisation check at the card processor, store rules per card, do atomic checks with currency conversion, return decline codes and messages, add an admin UI and audit logs, handle offline or partial authorisations, test and monitor fraud. Limits are enforced in real time.
What are the key requirements for a SaaS product integrating with a cloud marketplace?

A startup wants to sell through a cloud provider's marketplace. Typically: partner registration and tax and banking setup, product listing and pricing model, SSO and account linking, metering or usage-reporting APIs, SaaS fulfilment and subscription lifecycle events, security and compliance review and support obligations. I'd verify the current marketplace documentation for exact requirements.
How will you address your API limits? Describe scenarios across customers, technology and suppliers.

A provider's API quota is almost exhausted at peak. For customers: per-plan quotas, clear communication and queued work. For technology: caching, batching, backoff, priority queues and usage monitoring with alerts. For suppliers: negotiate higher limits, use multiple providers and have fallback modes. I'd track utilisation and test peak load.
How would you check for bias in your data, and what happens with excessive data or too few survey respondents?

To check bias, I'd compare data distribution to the target population, check missing groups and label quality, and test model outcomes by group. With too few survey respondents, I'd widen channels, add incentives, weight carefully and state the limits. Excess data collection creates privacy and cost risk, fatigue and regulatory exposure, so collect only what's needed.
An engineer wants a major ranking algorithm change. How would you evaluate it?

Search results may improve for some and worsen for others. I'd use offline metrics like NDCG on labelled sets, replay on logs, human evaluation, then an online A/B test with guardrails on latency, revenue and complaints, segment analysis and a ramp with rollback. It ships safely.
Explain a technical concept (cloud computing, an operating system, prime numbers, deep learning, or your analysis methods) to a non-technical person.

I start with their world. Cloud computing is like renting electricity instead of owning a power plant: you rent computers over the internet. An operating system is the manager that lets apps share the machine's parts. Prime numbers are numbers divisible only by 1 and themselves, like blocks that can't be split into equal smaller piles. Deep learning is a system that learns patterns from many examples, like a child learning to recognise cats. Then I'd ask a question to check they got it, so they can say it back in their own words.
Why is AI necessary here instead of rules, search, or a normal workflow?

I'd start by asking what job we're really solving and what the cheapest thing is that could solve it. Say a support team wants an LLM to route tickets. I'd look at the data first: if 90% of tickets contain ten obvious keywords, a rule does that for almost no cost and never surprises anyone. AI earns its place where the input is messy or open-ended, like free-text complaints, long documents or images, and where rules measurably fail. So I'd test rules against about a hundred real tickets, and only add an LLM for the messy 10%. That way I can show finance exactly what the AI adds and what it costs per request.
How would you know this LLM feature is good enough to launch?

I wouldn't judge it from a demo, because demos are hand-picked. Before launch I'd agree on a bar with the team, for example "90% of drafts are usable, under 1% are harmful, and p95 latency is under four seconds." Then I'd build an eval set of a few hundred real, messy inputs, run the feature against it, and compare it with what people do today. After that comes internal use, then a 5% canary with a rollback trigger written down in advance. If it clears the bar on real traffic, we ship; if not, we know exactly what to fix.
Design an AI assistant for customer support.

I'd begin with the tickets themselves: what are the top five reasons customers contact us, and which are safe to automate? Imagine a telecom where "reset my router" and "where is my bill" make up half the volume. The assistant would answer those from the help centre and read-only account data, ask for authentication first, and refuse anything risky like refunds above a limit. Anything it can't resolve goes to a human with a summary, so the customer never repeats themselves. I'd launch on those top intents, track resolution rate, satisfaction and cost per resolved ticket, and widen only when the numbers hold.
What failure would make you pause the launch or require human review?

I'd define those lines before launch, not during a crisis. Picture a loan-summary assistant that occasionally makes up an interest rate. I'd say any invented number is a stop-ship, more than half a percent policy-violating answers means human review, and a single privacy leak means we pause. Each trigger has an owner and a pre-agreed action. Then when it happens, the team acts in minutes instead of holding a meeting, and leadership trusts the launch because the limits were written down.
Helpful-completion rate improved, but harmful outputs also increased. What do you do?

I wouldn't average the two into one score. I'd first find where the harm sits: which topics or users. Say the red-team harm rate went from 0.3% to 1.1% while helpfulness rose. I'd look at severity, not just the rate, because a rude answer and a dangerous one are very different. Then I'd tighten the safety prompt, add a classifier on the risky topics, and retest. If severe harm stays above the threshold, I roll back or restrict that capability. The trade-off goes to leadership as an explicit decision, not a hidden side effect.
How do you prioritise AI features?

I'd score each idea on user impact, how often the problem occurs, data readiness, and how accurate the AI needs to be versus what's achievable. Then I'd add two AI-specific factors: how hard it is to evaluate, and how bad a failure would be. A quick prototype tells me feasibility faster than a meeting. I'd sequence one quick win first and one bigger bet second, so the team ships something real while learning about the harder problem.
How do you decide between building and buying (API) an AI capability?

I'd compare time to value, quality, cost at scale, data control and whether it differentiates us. For a non-core feature like summarising meeting notes, I'd buy through an API and be live in weeks. If our proprietary data is the moat, or privacy requires it, I'd consider building or fine-tuning. I'd keep an abstraction layer so we can switch vendors, and I'd revisit the decision as prices and models change.
Should this workflow use an agent?

I'd ask one question: do we know the steps in advance? Take expense approvals: extract the receipt, check it against policy, route to a manager. That's a fixed recipe, so I'd build a workflow, using the LLM only for the fuzzy bits like reading the receipt. An agent makes sense when the path really varies, like researching a company where each finding decides the next search. Agents cost more, run slower and are harder to debug, so I'd test both on fifty sample cases and pick the simpler one that is reliable enough.
How would you improve an AI search experience?

I'd start from the logs rather than from ideas: what are people searching for, how often do they get nothing, how often do they rephrase, what do they click? Suppose employees type questions but get ten blue links. I'd add semantic plus keyword search, rewrite vague queries, rerank the results, and put a short answer on top with citations so people can check it. I'd keep a plain link list as fallback. Success looks like fewer reformulations, more answered questions, and users trusting the answer enough to click the source.
What should the product refuse, or hand to a human?

I'd decide by risk and reversibility. Imagine a bank bot asked for investment advice, or from someone describing a relative's death. Those are cases where a wrong or tone-deaf answer does real damage, so the bot should decline politely or hand over to a person with the conversation attached. I'd write that policy down, test it with red-team prompts, and watch two numbers: how many risky cases slip through, and how often we refuse harmless questions. Both errors cost something, so I want to see both.
Which user segment should receive the first release?

I'd choose the group that teaches us the fastest at the lowest risk. For an AI writing tool that might be our own employees or a small group of friendly power users, not regulated or high-stakes users. They feel the pain, tolerate rough edges, and give honest feedback. Before launch I'd write down what we need to learn, say usage frequency and accuracy, and what result lets us widen the release. Then bugs hurt a few people, not everyone.
Your company spent a year on a GenAI product with no traction. Keep investing or kill it?

I'd separate the sunk cost from the future. I'd ask whether the problem is real, by looking at usage intent and workarounds, and whether the product or the idea is wrong. Then I'd propose a six to eight week test with a bar set in advance, for example "weekly active users retain at X%" or "task success reaches Y." If we miss it, we stop and move the team. If it partly works for one segment, we narrow to that segment. Either way I document the decision so the team isn't left guessing.
You have a technology that lets humans understand animals. What do you build?

I'd start by admitting I don't know how accurate such a technology is, so my first step is validation. Realistically I'd begin with pet owners, a low-stakes, high-emotion market: for example interpreting a dog's stress signals, with clear "not medical advice" wording. I'd test accuracy with vets and animal-behaviour researchers before making any claim. A subscription app is a cheap way to test demand, and vet partnerships add credibility. Only after that would I think about zoos or research use.
You have a magical technology that converts text to music. How would you take it to market?

I'd pick a niche where the quality is good enough today and the buyer is clear. Content creators who need royalty-clear background music fast are a good start: they'd otherwise spend hours searching libraries. I'd check training-data rights and offer clear commercial licences, because legal risk can kill the product. Pricing could be a subscription with generation credits. I'd measure tracks exported and repeat use, not just generations. Game studios and advertisers come later.
How would you launch a productivity product for a large AI assistant?

I'd first pin down the job, for example "give me a summary of my morning and what needs a reply." Then I'd launch as opt-in with low-risk suggestions only, and I'd favour precision: interrupt only when we're confident, because one irrelevant nudge teaches users to ignore all of them. I'd measure acceptance, dismissals and opt-outs, and roll out in cohorts. If acceptance is high and opt-outs low, we've earned permission to be more proactive.
A VC asks you to build an AI career coach. What is your pitch?

My pitch would be narrow: early-career job seekers and career switchers who get no feedback. The coach builds a personal plan, practises interviews, and reviews resumes against real job postings. The advantage is data on what actually led to interviews and offers, which a generic chatbot lacks. Revenue is freemium with a subscription, and I'd measure interviews landed, not chat sessions. I'd be upfront about risks: bad advice and bias, so we show sources and keep humans' final say.
Define goals and success metrics for AirPods with built-in voice AI.

I'd think about what makes earbuds different: hands-free, always near, and sensitive. So the goal is a trusted daily habit. I'd track weekly active users, tasks completed by voice, wake-word accuracy, time to first spoken word, and user-rated helpfulness. Guardrails matter as much: false activations, battery drain and privacy complaints. If I only chased engagement, I'd end up with a device that listens too eagerly and drains the battery.
How would you design an AI evaluation system for resumes?

I'd treat it as a fairness and accuracy problem together. First I'd build a labelled set from hiring-manager decisions and measure agreement and how many qualified candidates the tool surfaces. Then I'd check selection rates across groups and run counterfactual tests, like swapping names on the same resume. Humans keep the final decision and every score is logged. That way I can tell legal and leadership both that it's useful and that we monitor it for bias.
We launched an AI tutor feature. Under 10% find it magical and most find it useless. How do you fix it?

I'd stop looking at the average and look at who loves it. A 10% "magical" group is a signal. I'd segment users, read the conversation logs for failure types (wrong, generic, too long), and interview ten people from each group. Then I'd form hypotheses, for example it helps at homework time but not for open questions, and test the strongest one quickly. I'd build for the cohort that gets the magic first and decide later whether the rest are worth serving.
Notification engagement is up six weeks in a row but time on site is flat. What do you do?

That mismatch tells me notifications might be creating opens, not value. I'd break it down by notification type and cohort, then check what happens after the tap: do people stay, convert, or leave? I'd also look at opt-outs and uninstalls. The cleanest test is a holdout group with no notifications. If they retain just as well, we're making noise, and I'd shift the goal to something tied to real user value, like completed tasks.
Should we use an LLM or a classic ML model for this?

I'd go with whatever solves the task most cheaply and reliably. Take sorting support tickets into twelve labels: if we have thousands of labelled tickets, a classic classifier is usually faster, cheaper and more consistent than an LLM. LLMs shine when data is scarce or the output is open-ended, like drafting a reply. So I'd compare accuracy, cost, latency and explainability on a sample, and often use the small model for routing and the LLM for the writing.
How would you launch an AI product with low accuracy?

I'd position it as an assistant, not an authority. If a tool is right 70% of the time, it shouldn't act alone; it should draft, suggest and show sources and confidence so the user can verify. I'd keep humans on high-risk steps, make corrections one click, and start with a small group. Every correction becomes training signal. Users save time because mistakes are caught by design, and accuracy improves with real usage.
How do you handle the cold start problem in a recommendation product?

With no history, I'd lean on what I do know: popular items in the user's country and time of day, a few onboarding questions, and content similarity. A new streaming user might pick three shows they like, and that's enough to start. I'd also reserve some slots for exploration so the system learns fast, then shift to personal signals as data arrives. The test is whether new users find something to watch in the first session.
What makes a great AI product manager?

I think a great AI PM is someone who can define "good" for a probabilistic product. They understand users deeply, know enough about models to challenge the team, and are comfortable with uncertainty. For example, they write the eval set together with the team before building, so everyone knows what success looks like. They also think about cost, risk and trust from day one, and they can explain trade-offs to executives in plain words.
How is an AI product different from a traditional product?

The biggest difference is that outputs are probabilistic, so quality is a distribution, not pass or fail. That changes the process: evals replace many test cases, costs scale with usage, data becomes a product asset, and new failure modes like hallucination and bias appear. Launches are staged with monitoring and rollback because behaviour can change when the model does. I'd explain it to a team as "we ship a system that we measure continuously, not a feature we test once."
How do you work with data scientists and ML engineers?
